source.title: Regularising for invariance to data augmentation improves supervised learning
source.authors: Aleksander Botev; M. Bauer; Soham De

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether an explicit invariance regularizer and augmentation multiplicity affect supervised test performance, using a KL-based measure of prediction invariance. These are conceptually related to generalization and regularization, but do not test the specific behaviors or measures in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-accuracy and invariance results for multiple-augmentation objectives and a KL regularizer. Its main numerical table reports central-crop test accuracy. Other reported accuracy trends are shown in figures and described in text. Dropout is part of some training recipes but is not varied.
record.test_reason: The study tests augmentation objectives and prediction-invariance regularization, not V1–V8. Its width sweep does not establish zero training error or widening beyond an interpolation threshold (V2). Total batch size is fixed and epoch budgets are tuned separately, so augmentation multiplicity is not a test of V5. Dropout is not varied, and prediction invariance is not weight-perturbation sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the authors' qualitative conclusion: averaging individual augmentation losses yields better generalization and more invariant individual predictions than averaging logits or probabilities; explicitly regularizing prediction agreement improves performance and largely equalizes the objectives. Their proposed explanation concerns invariance of individual predictions. It does not establish any of V1–V8.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies data-augmentation objectives and a predictive-distribution KL regularizer, rather than random-label memorization, interpolation width, optimizer choice, batch size, dropout intervention, sharpness, or memorized-example removal. It uses SGD with momentum and natural image datasets; random-label fitting is not tested.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with augmentation multiplicity, objective, dataset and model. The paper reports that the batch-normalized ResNet-18 reproduces some trends that differ from the normalizer-free models; it notes that ghost batch size was not swept. Regularizer strength also affects accuracy, with λ = 0 markedly worse and very large values degrading accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: At the reported augmentation multiplicities, averaging losses outperforms averaging probabilities or logits. Adding the KL regularizer improves central-crop accuracy for all three objectives and largely equalizes their performance across the three Table 1 models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Encouraging agreement between predictions for different augmentations can improve supervised image-classification accuracy and reduce differences among augmentation objectives.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing WideResNet width or depth improves baseline test accuracy on CIFAR-100; regularized models improve approximately in parallel. The text's gap here is between regularized and unregularized accuracy, not a training–test generalization gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across the tested WideResNet capacities, increasing width or depth improves held-out accuracy while preserving a similar accuracy benefit from prediction-invariance regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing augmentation multiplicity hurts the Bayesian-inspired objectives in normalizer-free models, whereas batch-normalized ResNet-18 shows improvements for the probability objective and part of the logit-objective range.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of augmentation multiplicity on held-out accuracy depends on the objective and architecture or normalization setup.

record.problems: ImageNet experiments use a single seed. Experiments are limited to classification on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet with selected model families and augmentation pipelines. The authors note that ghost batch size was not swept in the batch-normalized ResNet-18 comparison. Several additional findings are figure-only; the NFNet-F0 regularized entries in the flattened Table 1 cannot be confidently assigned.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-based numerical results for augmentation multiplicity, width/depth, regularizer strength, and the ResNet-18 comparison are not extracted as rows because values are figure-only or not given numerically in text. Table 1's NFNet-F0 regularized values are not assigned because its flattened layout does not support reliable mapping.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy, and their coexistence under the same recipe.
Widening beyond the width needed for zero training error. The convolutional width sweep reports test accuracy without establishing interpolation and uses explicit weight decay and augmentation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, local connectivity, and convolution-derived initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning or recovery recipes.
Larger versus smaller total batches under matched epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a large-batch penalty.
Adding or removing dropout, varying dropout strength or training-set size, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with train–test gaps, and comparison with norm or margin measures.
Removing highly memorized versus randomly selected training examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 has four accuracy columns: Ktrain=1 reference, then averaged losses, probabilities, and logits at Ktrain=16 or 8. The extraction shifted these columns and misassigned several values across models. Table 2 independently confirms the WRN and NF-ResNet mappings. All states remain cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 despite readable accuracy values. These are comparisons of the study's methods, so they should not serve as claim-evidence rows. Figure-only results are already declared in rows_left_out; no omitted result establishes a claim version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; random-label held-out performance.
Zero-training-error interpolation threshold and test error as width grows beyond it.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and their held-out performance.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout intervention and its effect across training-set sizes or dropout strengths.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness and comparison with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
